title: Term 3 and 4 Examination
instructions: This paper covers the work of Term 3. Term 4 is set aside for revision and the final examinations.
This question paper consists of 4 questions. Answer ALL the questions.
Read each question carefully before you answer it.

sections.title: QUESTION 1: Unseen Poetry
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: "Hope" is the thing with feathers – Emily Dickinson (published 1891; public domain)
context.text:
"Hope" is the thing with feathers -
That perches in the soul -
And sings the tune without the words -
And never stops - at all -

And sweetest - in the Gale - is heard -
And sore must be the storm -
That could abash the little Bird
That kept so many warm -

I've heard it in the chillest land -
And on the strangest Sea -
Yet - never - in Extremity,
It asked a crumb - of me.

questions.prompt: To what is hope compared throughout the poem?
A metaphor developed over a whole poem is called…
Each stanza of the poem has four lines. Such a stanza is called a…
The speaker suggests that hope is heard most sweetly during difficult times.
Explain the meaning of stanza 2, referring to 'Gale' and 'storm'.
questions.memo:
✓ The gale/storm symbolises hardship or suffering (1)
✓ Hope is strongest ('sweetest') in those times (1)
✓ Only an extremely severe crisis could silence it, and it has comforted ('kept warm') many people (1)

questions.prompt: What does the final line, 'It asked a crumb - of me', reveal about hope?
questions.memo:
✓ Hope is selfless and asks nothing in return (1)
✓ The image of a crumb continues the bird metaphor (1)

questions.prompt: How does the third stanza differ from the first two?
questions.memo:
✓ The speaker introduces personal experience ('I've heard it') (1)
✓ 'Yet' signals the final point about hope's selflessness (1)

questions.prompt: About how long should the Grade 12 poetry essay be?
What is the one-sentence statement of your argument in the introduction called?
Events in a literary text are usually discussed in the present tense.
The conclusion is the best place to introduce a new, important point.
Match each part of a PEEL paragraph to its purpose.

pairs.right: Topic sentence linked to the thesis
Analysis of how the evidence proves the point

questions.prompt: Write ONE PEEL paragraph on the theme of power in 'Ozymandias'.
questions.memo:
✓ Point linked to power (1)
✓ Embedded quotation, e.g. 'King of Kings' or 'Nothing beside remains' (1)
✓ Explanation of effect (1)
✓ Link to the theme of impermanence (1)

sections.title: QUESTION 3: Reflective Essays and Visual Prompts

questions.prompt: Which statement best describes the main purpose of a reflective essay?
options: To tell an exciting story with a clear climax and resolution
To explore the personal meaning of an experience or idea and show what the writer has come to understand
To convince the reader to accept one side of a debatable issue
To create a vivid picture of a place using the five senses
questions.explanation: A reflective essay asks ‘What did it mean, and how has it changed my thinking?’ The other options describe narrative, argumentative and descriptive essays.

questions.prompt: A reflective essay is mainly a retelling of events in time order, with a short lesson added in the final sentence.
questions.explanation: That is a mere narrative with a moral. In a reflective essay, events are told briefly and reflection runs through the whole essay.

questions.prompt: In the CAPS Home Language essay rubric (out of 50), how many marks are allocated to **Content and planning**? Give a whole number.
questions.explanation: Content and planning 30, Language, style and editing 15, Structure 5: a total of 50.

questions.prompt: What is the recommended length for the Home Language essay in Paper 3 Section A?
questions.explanation: The HL essay is 400–450 words. 180–200 words is the length of an HL transactional text in Section B.

questions.prompt: Apart from the number of the topic, what must you always give your essay, especially when you respond to a visual prompt?
questions.explanation: The paper requires you to give your essay a suitable title. For pictures this is essential, because the title shows how you have interpreted the image.

questions.prompt: Match each topic with the essay type it most clearly calls for.

pairs.left: ‘Social media does more harm than good.’ Do you agree?
Describe a busy taxi rank at dawn.
Write a story that ends with: ‘And that was the last time I saw him.’
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of a four-day school week.
Looking back on the moment I stopped being a child

questions.explanation: ‘Do you agree?’ asks for a one-sided argument; ‘describe’ asks for description; a given ending line asks for a story; ‘advantages and disadvantages’ asks for a balanced discussion; ‘looking back’ asks for reflection.

questions.prompt:
Rewrite the following narrative paragraph as a **reflective** paragraph of about 80–100 words. Keep the event brief and add feeling, thought and insight.

‘On the day of the inter-schools athletics final, I lined up for the 800 metres. The gun went off and I ran as fast as I could. In the final bend I tripped over another runner’s foot and fell. Everyone stared. I got up and finished last. Then we went home.’
questions.memo:
Model answer:
‘I still remember the gravel in my palms more clearly than the race itself. In the final bend of the 800 metres I fell, and for a few seconds the whole stadium seemed to hold its breath. At the time, finishing last felt like the end of the world; I was sure everyone would remember my fall for ever. Looking back, I realise that nobody remembers it but me. What I do remember is choosing to get up. I have come to understand that people rarely judge us for falling; they notice whether we finish.’

Mark allocation:
✓ The event is reduced to a brief, concrete anchor; unnecessary actions such as ‘Then we went home’ are cut (1)
✓ Feelings or beliefs at the time are expressed (1)
✓ A clear shift to present understanding, e.g. ‘Looking back, I realise…’ (1)
✓ A specific, earned insight rather than a cliché such as ‘I learnt never to give up’ (1)
✓ First person, sincere tone, correct language and roughly 80–100 words (1)

sections.title: QUESTION 4: Articles, Dialogues, Interviews and Minutes
sections.instructions: Read the text below, then answer the questions.

context.title: Opening of a model column (written for this guide)
context.text:
SIPHO SPEAKS
This week: In defence of the humble taxi queue

I have stood in a lot of queues in my life, but none has taught me more about South Africa than the queue at Bree Street taxi rank at half past five on a Friday. Strangers share umbrellas. A gogo keeps your place while you buy a vetkoek. Nobody pushes, because everyone is equally tired. If our politicians want to learn about patience and fairness, I suggest they start here…

questions.prompt: Which of the following is the most effective **newspaper headline**?
options: The learners of a school in Durban who cleaned a beach on Saturday morning.
Dear readers, a beach has been cleaned!
Durban learners clear 500 kg of plastic from beach
questions.explanation: A headline is short and specific, uses the present tense and an active verb, leaves out small words and has no full stop.

questions.prompt: What should the lead (first) paragraph of a newspaper article do?
options: Answer the key questions: who, what, when, where, why and how
Give the journalist’s personal opinion of the event
Provide the background history before mentioning the event
Thank readers for buying the newspaper
questions.explanation: The lead sums up the story by answering the 5 Ws and H. A news article is objective, and background comes later in the inverted pyramid.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the news-writing structure in which the most important information comes first and less important details follow?
questions.explanation: The inverted pyramid puts the key facts at the top so that the story still makes sense if the end is cut.

questions.prompt: In a dialogue, each speaker’s words are placed in inverted commas.
questions.explanation: A dialogue is set out like a script: the speaker’s name, a colon and then the words, with no inverted commas.

questions.prompt: Minutes of a meeting are usually written in the past tense, in the third person, using reported speech.
questions.explanation: Minutes are a formal record written after the meeting, e.g. ‘Ms Pillay reported that the principal had approved the date.’

questions.prompt: Match each feature with the text type it belongs to.

pairs.left: Catchy title, subheadings and a chatty tone that addresses readers as ‘you’
Date at the top, first person and private feelings
Numbered steps beginning with imperative verbs
Prepared open questions put to a person, with a polite opening and thanks at the end

questions.explanation: Each text type has signature features: minutes record procedure and decisions; news uses a lead and inverted pyramid; magazine articles are chatty; diaries are private and dated; instructions use imperatives; interviews are built on open questions.

questions.prompt: How does a newspaper **column** differ from a newspaper **article**?
options: A column is a regular feature in which a named columnist gives a personal opinion in a distinctive voice, while an article reports facts objectively.
A column always uses the inverted pyramid, while an article never does.
A column is written in the third person and never contains the writer’s opinion.
A column is the headline printed above an article.
questions.explanation: Columns are subjective, usually in the first person and appear regularly under the columnist’s name. News articles are objective reports.
